title: Ang 795: Bilaval begins
hook: Guru Nanak opens the morning raga of joy
tomorrow: can you feel joy and miss someone on the same morning?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Farid: build the raft now, in calm water, before the lake rises. Today a new raga starts, and it starts in the morning.

Call a CEO "team lead" and watch the face. A title that's too small can sting more than no title at all. That's how Guru Nanak opens raga Bilaval, on ang 795. In paraphrase: you are the Sultan; if I call you chief, what kind of praise is that? Every word he has is too small for God. His answer to that problem isn't silence. It's to sing anyway.
screen: `TOO SMALL A TITLE.` → `YOU ARE THE SULTAN.` → `SING ANYWAY.`

segments.voice: Bilaval is sung as a morning raga, and Sikh tradition hears joy in it. Guru Nanak's opening hymn, in paraphrase: you are the Sultan, and I call you chief; what greatness is that? Whatever you give me, I speak; I'm a fool, I can't find the words. Then the refrain asks: give me understanding, so I can sing your praises and live in your will. So the joy here isn't the joy of getting it right. It's praising when the words don't fit. And this morning raga opens a real conversation among Sikhs today. Some kirtan teachers say gurbani should be sung in its own raga, the one named above each hymn, because the Gurus set the music with the words: Bilaval for a morning's joy. Lose the raga, they say, and part of the meaning goes quiet. Others say a simple, familiar tune lets more people sing along, and the shabad matters more than the scale. A hymn nobody joins in on, they say, has also lost something. Both sides love the same hymns, and both are trying to keep them alive. And Guru Nanak's own words sit right between them: any title is too small, so sing with what you have, and ask for understanding.
screen: `YOU ARE THE SULTAN; I SAY CHIEF.` · `GIVE ME UNDERSTANDING TO SING.` · `KEEP THE RAGA THE GURUS SET.` · `OR A TUNE EVERYONE CAN SING.` · then, large: `MORNING JOY.`

segments.voice: Listen for one sound around you right now: a bird, a fan, traffic, someone in the next room. Rest your attention on it for the sit, and let it be your morning raga, whatever time it is. If you'd like, read Guru Nanak's opening hymn on ang 795 first.
Ang 795. Where raga Bilaval begins, with Guru Nanak's hymn about praise that's always too small.
Morning joy: the words are too small, so sing with the ones you have. Bilaval has begun.

howItsDone: Each section of the Guru Granth Sahib is headed by its raga; in many gurdwaras ragis sing Bilaval's hymns in the morning, and Sikhs today debate how strictly kirtan should keep to the named raga.

Bilaval.meaning: a raga of the Granth, sung in the morning

kirtan.meaning: singing the Granth's hymns, usually with music

gurbani.meaning: the Gurus' words, the hymns of the Granth

shabad.meaning: a hymn of the Granth; also, the Word

raga.meaning: a musical mode; the Granth is arranged by them
